Navigating the AI Accountability Gap - Who Pays When the Algorithm Fails? 
Navigating the "accountability gap" in artificial intelligence requires rethinking traditional legal paradigms as AI transitions from automated task execution to autonomous decision-making. When an AI system causes harm whether through autonomous vehicle collisions, medical misdiagnoses or algorithmic discrimination traditional legal doctrines face profound friction. 
Classical tort law relies on human intent, duty of care, negligence and foreseeability. However, deep learning models present a fundamental evidentiary hurdle which is the Black Box Problem. Because multi-layered neural networks operate non-linearly, tracing an autonomous output back to a specific human act or design flaw becomes exceedingly difficult. This renders the standard of foreseeability elusive and complicates establishing causation. 
Doctrinal Applications & Allocating Liability
Courts and scholars are evaluating several traditional frameworks to address AI harm 
Product Liability vs. Services - Treating AI as a product enables strict liability, holding developers or manufacturers accountable without requiring proof of fault. However, software-as-a-service (SaaS) models often blur the distinction between a product and a service, complicating strict liability claims. 
Negligence & The "Reasonable Developer" Standard - Standard tort principles require proving a breach of duty. Modern jurisprudence is moving toward establishing a "reasonable AI developer" benchmark for testing, algorithmic auditing, and deployment oversight. 
Vicarious Liability & Quasi-Agency - While vicarious liability traditionally applies to human agents, adapting this model requires treating AI systems as quasi-agents or attributing operational liability directly to the principal controller. 
Allocation of Risk - In complex multi-stakeholder supply chains (comprising data annotators, model developers, fine-tuners, and end-users) liability allocation often turns on the Cheapest Cost Avoider principle says placing primary responsibility on the party best positioned to prevent the harm. Alternatively, joint and several liability ensures injured parties are made whole. 
Jurisdictional Approaches & Future Frameworks
Globally, regulatory strategies are diverging. The European Union leads with a risk-based regime under the EU AI Act and updated Product Liability Directives, establishing strict oversight and shifting or easing burdens of proof for high-risk applications. In contrast, the United States largely relies on state-level legislation and evolving common law tort litigation. 
The Information Technology Act, 2000 focuses on human intermediary liability rather than autonomous algorithmic fault.
